items.stem:
Read the following final stanza of "The Mask of Anarchy" (1819) by Percy Bysshe Shelley.

Rise like Lions after slumber
In unvanquishable number—
Shake your chains to earth like dew
Which in sleep had fallen on you—
Ye are many—they are few.

Explain how the form of this poem contributes to its meaning.
items.answer: Form: rhyming couplets and a final triplet (slumber/number, dew/you/few) in a strong trochaic rhythm, giving the stanza the force of a chant or rallying cry.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Traditional forms like the sonnet are less suitable than free verse for modern protest poetry."
items.answer: Both can work; the best choice depends on whether the poet wants order to contrast with chaos or form to mirror disruption.

items.stem:
Read the following poem about leaving home, from a contemporary anthology.

Departure Lounge

My mother packed the spices first –
cardamom, turmeric, a jar of chilli
wrapped in a jumper like a sleeping child –
as if a country could be carried
in small glass jars.

At the gate, she did not look back.
I did. I am still
looking.

Describe the tone of the text and explain how the writer creates it.
items.answer: The tone is wistful: tender sensory details and the lingering final line create a wistful tone.
items.markingKey: The tone is wistful: tender sensory details and the lingering final line create a wistful tone. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following poem written to be performed at a youth protest march.

They told us to wait.
We waited through three elections,
two floods and one fire season
that never really ended.

They told us to be realistic.
We are. We have done the maths.

They told us we were too young to understand.
We understand this:
you can't negotiate with a thermometer.

So we are done waiting.
Look out of your windows.
We are the weather now.

Identify the technique used in "They told us to wait. ... They told us to be realistic. ... They told us we were too young" and explain its effect.
items.answer: Anaphora: "They told us to wait. ... They told us to be realistic. ... They told us we were too young" – the repeated opening lists adult excuses, each one rejected in turn.
items.markingKey: Anaphora: "They told us to wait. ... They told us to be realistic. ... They told us we were too young" – the repeated opening lists adult excuses, each one rejected in turn. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). items.stem:
Read the following free-verse poem about a girl crossing a checkpoint on her way to school.

Every morning she shows them
her bag:
a pencil case, a maths book,
an apple she will not eat until noon.

They search it like a country
they suspect of hiding something.

She has learned to stand still,
to look at the middle distance,
to keep her homework dry
and her anger folded
small enough to fit
between the pages.

items.stem:
Read the following final lines of the sonnet "Ozymandias" (1818) by Percy Bysshe Shelley.

And on the pedestal, these words appear:
My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings;
Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare
The lone and level sands stretch far away.

Explain how the form of this poem shapes its meaning, and suggest how a poem on a similar theme might use a different form.
items.answer: Form: the lines come from a sonnet in iambic pentameter with an unusual, interlocking rhyme scheme; the volta turns from the tyrant's boast to the emptiness around it. Enjambement ("Round the decay / Of that colossal Wreck") makes the sands seem to stretch across the line break.

Enjambement ("Round the decay / Of that colossal Wreck") makes the sands seem to stretch across the line break. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Text A: free-verse poem about a girl crossing a checkpoint on her way to school.

Every morning she shows them
her bag:
a pencil case, a maths book,
an apple she will not eat until noon.

They search it like a country
they suspect of hiding something.

She has learned to stand still,
to look at the middle distance,
to keep her homework dry
and her anger folded
small enough to fit
between the pages.

Text B: sonnet about a city divided by a wall.

They built the wall the summer I was born,
a seam of grey that stitched the city through;
my mother's sister waved across the thorn
of wire, and every year the distance grew.
We learned the shapes of windows on that side,
the radio songs we were not meant to hear,
the names of streets where cousins lived and died
so close, so far, a whisper and a year.
But walls are only stone, and stone grows old;
one night the crowd came singing with their hands,
and pulled the grey apart, and through the cold
two sisters met like strangers from two lands.
  They held each other, laughing, wet with rain –
  then, slowly, learned each other's names again.

Compare how the two poems present the effects of division and conflict on ordinary people. Consider form, imagery and tone.
items.answer: Both poems present conflict through its effect on daily and family life rather than battles. "Checkpoint" uses free verse, a list of school objects and the simile "like a country / they suspect" to show a child treated as a threat; her anger is "folded / small enough to fit / between the pages". The sonnet uses the metaphor of a "seam of grey" stitching the city and the antithesis "so close, so far", with a volta ("But walls are only stone") leading to reunion. "Checkpoint" ends with suppressed anger in an ongoing situation; the sonnet ends with a bittersweet resolution, as sisters "learned each other's names again". Free verse suits ongoing tension, while the sonnet's ordered form suits a story with an ending.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Both poems present conflict through its effect on daily and family life rather than battles. "Checkpoint" uses free verse, a list of school objects and the simile "like a country / they suspect" to show a child treated as a threat; her anger is "folded / small enough to fit / between the pages". The sonnet uses the metaphor of a "seam of grey" stitching the city and the antithesis "so close, so far", with a volta ("But walls are only stone") leading to reunion. "Checkpoint" ends with suppressed anger in an ongoing situation; the sonnet ends with a bittersweet resolution, as sisters "learned each other's names again". Free verse suits ongoing tension, while the sonnet's ordered form suits a story with an ending. Comparison must be sustained across both texts (criterion B).

Text B: letter written in 1962 by a young woman who had recently emigrated, to her sister.

Dear Nalini,
The flat is small and the radiator knocks all night like a neighbour who wants to come in. At the factory they call me "Nelly" because they cannot say my name. I let them.
I have found a shop that sells cardamom, but it tastes of the box it came in.
Do not tell Amma I cry on the bus. Tell her I have a warm coat and that the English are polite. Both are true.
Your loving sister,
Saroja

items.answer: Running lines on delays meaning and creates momentum or a held breath across the line break.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Running lines on delays meaning and creates momentum or a held breath across the line break. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between alliteration and assonance.
items.answer: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds at the start of words; assonance repeats vowel sounds within words.
items.markingKey: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds at the start of words; assonance repeats vowel sounds within words. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the poet and the speaker.
items.answer: The poet is the writer; the speaker is the voice in the poem, which may be a persona.
items.markingKey: The poet is the writer; the speaker is the voice in the poem, which may be a persona. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following poem about leaving home, from a contemporary anthology.

Departure Lounge

My mother packed the spices first –
cardamom, turmeric, a jar of chilli
wrapped in a jumper like a sleeping child –
as if a country could be carried
in small glass jars.

At the gate, she did not look back.
I did. I am still
looking.

Explain how the form of this poem shapes its meaning, and suggest how a poem on a similar theme might use a different form.
items.answer: Form: free verse in two stanzas; the enjambement and the final one-word line ("looking.") make the speaker's backward glance last beyond the poem.
items.markingKey: Form: free verse in two stanzas; the enjambement and the final one-word line ("looking.") make the speaker's backward glance last beyond the poem. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following sonnet about a city divided by a wall.

They built the wall the summer I was born,
a seam of grey that stitched the city through;
my mother's sister waved across the thorn
of wire, and every year the distance grew.
We learned the shapes of windows on that side,
the radio songs we were not meant to hear,
the names of streets where cousins lived and died
so close, so far, a whisper and a year.
But walls are only stone, and stone grows old;
one night the crowd came singing with their hands,
and pulled the grey apart, and through the cold
two sisters met like strangers from two lands.
  They held each other, laughing, wet with rain –
  then, slowly, learned each other's names again.

How does the final rhyming couplet shape the reader's experience of the text?
items.answer: The final rhyming couplet: the couplet's image of re-learning names shows that reunion does not erase the damage of division.
items.markingKey: The final rhyming couplet: the couplet's image of re-learning names shows that reunion does not erase the damage of division. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following free-verse poem about a girl crossing a checkpoint on her way to school.

Every morning she shows them
her bag:
a pencil case, a maths book,
an apple she will not eat until noon.

They search it like a country
they suspect of hiding something.

She has learned to stand still,
to look at the middle distance,
to keep her homework dry
and her anger folded
small enough to fit
between the pages.

Describe the tone of the text and explain how the writer creates it.
items.answer: The tone is restrained and indignant: calm, plain description barely holds back anger at injustice.
items.markingKey: The tone is restrained and indignant: calm, plain description barely holds back anger at injustice. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Identify the tone of "Checkpoint" and quote two details that create it.
items.answer: Restrained/indignant: "She has learned to stand still"; "her anger folded / small enough to fit".
items.markingKey: Restrained/indignant: "She has learned to stand still"; "her anger folded / small enough to fit".

items.stem:
Read the following final stanza of "The Mask of Anarchy" (1819) by Percy Bysshe Shelley.

Rise like Lions after slumber
In unvanquishable number—
Shake your chains to earth like dew
Which in sleep had fallen on you—
Ye are many—they are few.

Explain how the form of this poem shapes its meaning, and suggest how a poem on a similar theme might use a different form.
items.answer: Form: rhyming couplets and a final triplet (slumber/number, dew/you/few) in a strong trochaic rhythm, giving the stanza the force of a chant or rallying cry.
items.markingKey: Form: rhyming couplets and a final triplet (slumber/number, dew/you/few) in a strong trochaic rhythm, giving the stanza the force of a chant or rallying cry. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

Analyse how the poet uses structure and line breaks for effect.
items.answer: Form: free verse with no regular rhyme or metre; short, uneven lines and enjambement ("shows them / her bag") create pauses that mimic the stop-start of the checkpoint and the girl's careful self-control.

items.stem:
Read the following poem about leaving home, from a contemporary anthology.

Departure Lounge

My mother packed the spices first –
cardamom, turmeric, a jar of chilli
wrapped in a jumper like a sleeping child –
as if a country could be carried
in small glass jars.

At the gate, she did not look back.
I did. I am still
looking.

How does the poet present the experience of leaving home? Focus on imagery and sound.
items.answer: Leaving home is presented through sensory, domestic details: the spices are "wrapped in a jumper like a sleeping child", a simile that shows how precious the homeland's tastes are. The conceit "as if a country could be carried / in small glass jars" is touching but impossible. The contrast between the mother who "did not look back" and the speaker, and the shift into the present "I am still / looking", shows that for the speaker the departure has never ended.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Leaving home is presented through sensory, domestic details: the spices are "wrapped in a jumper like a sleeping child", a simile that shows how precious the homeland's tastes are. The conceit "as if a country could be carried / in small glass jars" is touching but impossible. The contrast between the mother who "did not look back" and the speaker, and the shift into the present "I am still / looking", shows that for the speaker the departure has never ended. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: "Poetry can change the world." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Poetry rarely changes events alone, but it can shape feelings and memory and inspire people who do.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: poems inspire movements and are quoted at protests; they create empathy. Arguments against: laws and actions change the world, not words alone; many readers never see protest poems. Supported judgement: Poetry rarely changes events alone, but it can shape feelings and memory and inspire people who do. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.
